## Main slide 01 · Title {.talk-slide data-section="Opening"}

- Opening question: why pay full-resolution cost while the latent is still mostly noise?
- Say: “Pyramid Flow uses one generative trajectory whose spatial resolution increases over time.”
- The same multiscale idea also compresses older temporal context.
- Talk order: algorithm, repository implementation, then live demonstration.

<div class="pace-cue"><span>0:00–0:30</span></div>

## Main slide 02 · Paper structure {.talk-slide data-section="Roadmap"}

- The talk follows the paper’s structure rather than the implementation order.
- Motivation and flow matching establish why a multiresolution path is possible.
- The central method consists of spatial stages, unified training, and re-noised transitions.
- The video extension compresses older history while maintaining causal generation.
- Experiments and repository code show what the abstraction buys in practice.

<div class="pace-cue"><span>0:30–1:00</span><em>compress to one sentence if late</em></div>

## Main slide 03 · Earlier design compromises {.talk-slide data-section="Introduction"}

- A 10-second clip at 24 fps is already 240 frames before repeated model evaluations.
- The VAE compresses pixels, but the DiT still revisits a large spatiotemporal token grid.
- A single full-resolution path pays the largest attention and memory cost from the first noisy state, limiting batch size, duration, or output resolution.
- Cascades avoid some of that cost, but introduce separate objectives and checkpoints with weaker parameter sharing between stages.
- Pyramid Flow is trying to keep the multiscale savings while sharing one end-to-end model.

<div class="pace-cue"><span>1:00–2:10</span></div>

## Main slide 04 · Early states need less detail {.talk-slide data-section="Introduction"}

- Read Figure 1 from left to right.
- In the conventional path, all frames remain at full spatial resolution even when dominated by noise.
- In the proposed path, global composition appears on a coarse grid before fine detail is introduced.
- This is not a separate super-resolution cascade.
- The stages form one continuous probability path trained by one model.

<div class="pace-cue"><span>2:10–3:10</span></div>

## Main slide 05 · How flow matching works {.talk-slide data-section="Preliminaries"}

- Training starts with Gaussian noise, a real video latent, and one random time between them.
- The intermediate state is `x_t = (1-t)x_0 + tx_1`; the supervised target is the endpoint difference `x_1 - x_0`.
- Training therefore needs one sampled point rather than simulating a complete denoising chain.
- Generation starts from noise and repeatedly evaluates the learned velocity while taking Euler steps.
- Connection to familiar models: iterative like diffusion, but the generative path is a deterministic ODE like a continuous flow.
- This formulation matters here because a path segment can connect representations at different resolutions.

<div class="pace-cue"><span>3:10–5:00</span></div>

## Main slide 06 · Spatial stages and boundaries {.talk-slide data-section="Method"}

- Divide one generative time interval into quarter-, half-, and full-resolution sections.
- Stage 1 handles composition and coarse motion; stage 2 resolves shapes and layout; stage 3 adds texture.
- One shared DiT works across all three sections—the timestep identifies the current stage.
- The hard part is every boundary: enlarge the grid, preserve the existing signal, and match the next noise covariance.
- A plain resize is therefore not a valid hand-off to the next stage.

<div class="pace-cue"><span>5:00–6:10</span></div>

- All three clips show the same generated scene after consecutive stages.
- At 160 × 96: global palette, perspective, composition, and rough motion are already present.
- At 320 × 192: objects, pedestrians, and scene layout become recognizable.
- At 640 × 384: edges, texture, faces, and smaller motion appear.
- Next question: how does one model learn a coherent path across those boundaries?

## Main slide 08 · Unified training {.talk-slide data-section="Method"}

- The graph reads left to right: clean video, VAE pyramid, sampled stage and time, coupled endpoints, shared DiT loss.
- The code is the same operation as the formula beside it: interpolate the endpoints and predict their difference.
- Notice the repository's sign convention: `target = start_point - end_point` because `r` decreases from 1 to 0.
- The learning rule is standard flow matching; the stage-specific endpoint construction is the innovation.
- Shared noise keeps adjacent stage distributions compatible and reduces conflicting paths.

<div class="pace-cue"><span>7:00–8:30</span></div>

## Main slide 09 · Inference with re-noising {.talk-slide data-section="Method"}

- Finish the Euler steps for the current stage before changing resolution.
- Nearest-neighbor upsampling copies each value into a 2 × 2 block.
- The signal survives, but the noise becomes perfectly correlated inside that block.
- The PyTorch excerpt shows the fix: resize, sample block noise, then combine both with `alpha` and `beta`.
- The added block noise has negative off-diagonal correlation within each 2 × 2 block, counteracting the duplicated upsampled noise.
- Together with `alpha` and `beta`, that matches the next stage's expected covariance.
- Without the correction, the next DiT evaluations would be off-distribution.

<div class="pace-cue"><span>8:30–10:00</span></div>

## Main slide 10 · Temporal pyramid {.talk-slide data-section="Video generation"}

- Spatial pyramids reduce the cost of the current unit; conditioning on history is a second token cost.
- Generation is autoregressive, so only completed units can condition the current one.
- Older units use a quarter grid—one sixteenth of the full spatial tokens per frame.
- The most recent unit stays at a half grid because local motion needs more detail.
- The current unit alone receives the full grid while it is being denoised.
- Tradeoff: cheaper long context, with a greater risk of long-term identity or scene drift.

<div class="pace-cue"><span>10:00–11:15</span></div>

## Main slide 11 · System architecture {.talk-slide data-section="Video generation"}

- Text encoder produces token-level and pooled prompt embeddings.
- Causal video VAE maps RGB frames to compact spatiotemporal latents and decodes the final latent.
- Temporal-pyramid logic packages earlier units at coarse or medium resolution.
- The shared DiT receives the current noisy latent, past conditions, timestep, and text; it outputs velocity.
- The Euler scheduler controls stage ranges, numerical steps, upsampling, and block-noise correction.
- The central model is not smaller or duplicated—the savings come from the token layout around it.

<div class="pace-cue"><span>11:15–12:15</span></div>

## Main slide 12 · Inference code walkthrough {.talk-slide data-section="Project"}

- The excerpt follows the control flow of `generate_one_unit()`.
- Outer loop: select the timestep schedule for each spatial stage.
- At later stages: nearest-neighbor upsample, sample block noise, then apply the `alpha`/`beta` correction.
- Inner loop: prepend the stage's temporal conditions, predict velocity with the DiT, and take one Euler step.
- Training-side construction lives in `add_pyramid_noise_with_temporal_pyramid()`; this slide focuses on inference.

## Main slide 13 · Controlled efficiency evidence {.talk-slide data-section="Experiments"}

- Lead with Figure 7 because it is controlled: the baseline uses the same data, tokens per batch, hyperparameters, and architecture.
- The pyramid curve reaches much better FID at the same training step; the paper describes almost three times faster convergence.
- Mechanism: most steps use fewer spatial tokens than full-resolution flow matching.
- The 20.7k A100 hours, 768p, 24 fps, and five- to ten-second figures describe the main model, not this ablation.
- Caveat: absolute GPU-hour comparisons still depend on utilization and software.

<div class="pace-cue"><span>13:15–14:30</span></div>

## Main slide 14 · Quality evidence {.talk-slide data-section="Experiments"}

- Read the selected rows rather than every benchmark entry.
- Gen-3 Alpha reports 82.32 total, 84.11 quality, 75.17 semantic, and 99.23 motion smoothness.
- VideoCrafter2 reports 80.44 / 82.20 / 73.42 / 97.73; T2V-Turbo reports 81.01 / 82.57 / 74.76 / 97.34 in the same column order.
- Pyramid Flow reports 81.72 total, 84.74 quality, 69.62 semantic, and 99.12 motion smoothness.
- Its semantic score is only 69.62, weaker than the comparison systems shown.
- The comparison supports a narrow claim: efficiency did not erase visual quality, but semantic alignment is not a strength.
- This is not a controlled comparison: data, scale, and infrastructure differ.

<div class="pace-cue"><span>14:30–15:30</span><em>skip table detail if late</em></div>

## Main slide 15 · Conclusion and limitations {.talk-slide data-section="Conclusion"}

- Central principle: match representation fidelity to the information present in the trajectory.
- The method shares one model across resolutions and compounds spatial and temporal savings.
- The same framework supports both text-to-video and image-to-video generation.
- Stage transitions add mathematical and implementation complexity.
- Autoregressive generation and compressed history can limit long-range consistency.
- Final quality still depends on the training data and the underlying DiT.
- Demo transition: the repository exposes these mechanisms in a runnable interface.

<div class="pace-cue"><span>15:30–16:15</span></div>
